Log-linear model of the test profiles

Source: R/loglinear.R
loglinear.Rd

Defines a model in which the distribution of the response profiles is log-linear in each disease class, so the dependence between the tests is restricted to interactions of at most interaction_order tests. The object is passed to baysesp() as its model argument.

Usage

loglinear(
  interaction_order = 1L,
  prevalence_prior = prior_beta(0.5, 2),
  sensitivity_prior = prior_beta(0.5, 2),
  specificity_prior = prior_beta(0.5, 2),
  interactions_prior = prior_normal(0, 1),
  verification = mar()
)

Arguments

interaction_order

A single whole number from 1 to the number of tests \(K\), the largest number of tests in an interaction. Default 1L (conditional independence). The lower bound is checked when the model is created; the upper bound is checked when the model is fitted.

prevalence_prior

Prior on the prevalence \(\pi\): a single prior, either on a probability, such as prior_beta(), which acts on \(\pi\), or on the real line, such as prior_normal(), which acts on \(\mathrm{logit}\,\pi\). Default prior_beta(0.5, 2), the uniform distribution on (0, 1).

sensitivity_prior, specificity_prior

Priors on the sensitivity and on the specificity of the tests: a single prior on a probability, prior_beta() or elicit_beta(), used for all tests, or a list with one such prior per test, in the order of the tests. Default prior_beta(0.5, 2), the uniform distribution on (0, 1). With interaction_order of 2 or more they act on conditional sensitivities and specificities: see the section "Priors on sensitivity and specificity".

interactions_prior

A single prior on the real line, applied to each class-specific interaction of order 2 or higher. Default prior_normal(0, 1). It has no effect when interaction_order = 1.

verification

The verification mechanism: mar() (default), with verification that depends only on the test profile, or mnar(), with verification that may also depend on the disease status.

Value

An object of class loglinear.

Details

Let \(K\) be the number of tests, \(t = (t_1, \dots, t_K)\) a response profile with \(t_k = 1\) for a positive result, \(d = 1\) for diseased and \(d = 0\) for healthy, and let \(m\) be interaction_order. For each disease class the profile probabilities \(\theta_d\) are $$\theta_d = \mathrm{softmax}(X_m \eta_d),$$ where \(X_m\) is the design matrix whose columns are the functions \(x_S(t) = \prod_{k \in S} t_k\), one for each set \(S\) of at most \(m\) tests, and \(\eta_d\) is the vector of the corresponding class-specific parameters \(\eta_{d,S}\). Equivalently, $$\theta_{d,t} \propto \exp\Big(\sum_{S} \eta_{d,S}\, x_S(t)\Big),$$ where the normalization runs over all \(2^K\) profiles. Log-linear models of this kind are used for multiple tests with partial verification (Baker, 1995).

The order controls the structure of the dependence:

  • Order 1 (interaction_order = 1): the tests are conditionally independent given the disease status.

  • Order 2: each pair of tests may be associated within each class, but there are no interactions among three or more tests.

  • Order \(K\): no restriction, every profile distribution is allowed in each class.

The parameters have a direct interpretation. With order 1, \(\eta_{1,k} = \mathrm{logit}(Se_k)\) and \(\eta_{0,k} = \mathrm{logit}(1 - Sp_k)\), so the main effects are the logits of the sensitivity and of the false positive rate of test \(k\). A pairwise term \(\eta_{d,\{j,k\}}\) is the log odds ratio between tests \(j\) and \(k\) within class \(d\), given the results of the other tests (with order 2 it is the same whatever those results; with higher orders it is the value when the other tests are negative): zero means that the two tests are independent within that class, positive values mean that they are positively associated among the diseased (\(d = 1\)) or among the healthy (\(d = 0\)). Ignoring the dependence between tests given the disease status biases the accuracy (Vacek, 1985; Torrance-Rynard and Walter, 1997; Dendukuri and Joseph, 2001).

The log-likelihood of the data, with \(n_{t,d}\) verified subjects of profile \(t\) and disease status \(d\), \(u_t\) unverified subjects of profile \(t\), \(\pi_1 = \pi\) the prevalence and \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi\), is $$\ell = \sum_t \Big[\sum_d n_{t,d} \log(\pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\,\lambda_{t,d}) + u_t \log \sum_d \pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\,(1 - \lambda_{t,d})\Big],$$ where \(\lambda_{t,d}\) is the probability of verification. Dependence models with partial verification of this kind are discussed by Albert and Dodd (2008). With verification = mar() the verification probability does not depend on the disease status given the profile (Rubin, 1976), so the verification term is separated from the disease model and can be ignored: $$\ell = \sum_t \Big[\sum_d n_{t,d} \log(\pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}) + u_t \log \sum_d \pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\Big]$$ plus a term that depends only on the verification probabilities. With verification = mnar() the verification probability may depend on the disease status (Baker, 1995; Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003): $$\mathrm{logit}\,\lambda_{t,d} = \alpha_t + \beta d,$$ with one \(\alpha_t\) for each verified profile. The parameter \(\beta\) is the log odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same profile, and \(\exp(-\beta)\) is the odds ratio of disease between unverified and verified subjects with the same profile. With verification = mnar(by_profile = TRUE) there is one \(\beta_t\) for each profile. Profiles that are never verified have \(\lambda_{t,d} = 0\).

With order lower than \(K\) the restricted structure also determines the disease proportion in the never-verified profiles, and makes \(\beta\) formally estimable. This information comes from the assumed structure, not from the data, and it is fragile if the structure is wrong (Albert and Dodd, 2004). With order \(K\) the model imposes no restriction and \(\beta\) is not identified (Gustafson, 2015).

Priors on sensitivity and specificity

The model is fitted on the main effects \(\eta_{d,k}\), and sensitivity_prior and specificity_prior are translated into priors on them. With interaction_order = 1 the main effects are the logits of the accuracy, $$\eta_{1,k} = \mathrm{logit}\,\mathrm{Se}_k, \qquad \eta_{0,k} = \mathrm{logit}(1 - \mathrm{Sp}_k),$$ so a prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)\) given to sensitivity_prior is the prior of \(\mathrm{Se}_k\), and one given to specificity_prior is the prior of \(\mathrm{Sp}_k\) (that is, \(\mathrm{Beta}(b, a)\) on the false positive rate \(1 - \mathrm{Sp}_k\)).

With interaction_order of 2 or more the main effects are logits of conditional probabilities: the probability that test \(k\) is positive among the subjects of class \(d\) who are negative on all the other tests, $$\mathrm{expit}\,\eta_{d,k} = P(T_k = 1 \mid D = d,\ T_j = 0 \ (j \neq k)).$$ So sensitivity_prior acts on the conditional sensitivity $$P(T_k = 1 \mid D = 1,\ T_j = 0 \ (j \neq k)) = \mathrm{expit}\,\eta_{1,k},$$ and specificity_prior on the conditional specificity $$P(T_k = 0 \mid D = 0,\ T_j = 0 \ (j \neq k)) = 1 - \mathrm{expit}\,\eta_{0,k},$$ not on the marginal \(\mathrm{Se}_k\) and \(\mathrm{Sp}_k\). The priors implied on the marginal sensitivity and specificity also depend on interactions_prior. With the default priors and three tests they are close to the uniform, but the interactions move the marginal sensitivity slightly up and the marginal specificity slightly down (medians about 0.54 and 0.46). An informative sensitivity_prior or specificity_prior should be set with this in mind.

References

Albert, P. S. and Dodd, L. E. (2004). A cautionary note on the robustness of latent class models for estimating diagnostic error without a gold standard. Biometrics, 60(2), 427–435. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2004.00187.x

Albert, P. S. and Dodd, L. E. (2008). On estimating diagnostic accuracy from studies with multiple raters and partial gold standard evaluation. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 103(481), 61–73. doi:10.1198/016214507000000329

Baker, S. G. (1995). Evaluating multiple diagnostic tests with partial verification. Biometrics, 51(1), 330–337. doi:10.2307/2533339

Dendukuri, N. and Joseph, L. (2001). Bayesian approaches to modeling the conditional dependence between multiple diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 57(1), 158–167. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00158.x

Gustafson, P. (2015). Bayesian Inference for Partially Identified Models: Exploring the Limits of Limited Data. Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL.

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003). Accounting for nonignorable verification bias in assessment of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 59(1), 163–171. doi:10.1111/1541-0420.00019

Rubin, D. B. (1976). Inference and missing data. Biometrika, 63(3), 581–592. doi:10.1093/biomet/63.3.581

Torrance-Rynard, V. L. and Walter, S. D. (1997). Effects of dependent errors in the assessment of diagnostic test performance. Statistics in Medicine, 16(19), 2157–2175. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19971015)16:19<2157::AID-SIM653>3.0.CO;2-X

Vacek, P. M. (1985). The effect of conditional dependence on the evaluation of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 41(4), 959–968. doi:10.2307/2530967

See also

saturated() for the model without restrictions on the profile distribution, mar() and mnar() for the verification mechanisms.

Examples

loglinear()                       # conditional independence
#> <loglinear> log-linear model of order 1
#>   prevalence_prior:   Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   sensitivity_prior:  Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   specificity_prior:  Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   interactions_prior: Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1)
#>   verification:       mar
loglinear(interaction_order = 2)  # pairwise dependence
#> <loglinear> log-linear model of order 2
#>   prevalence_prior:   Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   sensitivity_prior:  Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   specificity_prior:  Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   interactions_prior: Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1)
#>   verification:       mar
